senses: The Hawaiian duck, Anas wyvilliana.
ety: Borrowed from Hawaiian koloa, from Proto-Polynesian *toloa (“duck”).
examples: The Hawaiian duck or koloa (Anas wyvilliana) has never been reduced to anything like the pitiful remnant that once represented its relatives on Laysan.

senses: Each of the four members of a jointly ruling tetrarchy, notably of the Roman Empire since Diocletian.
An officer in charge of a fourth part of a phalanx in Ancient Greece.
ety: Borrowed from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).

senses: A marine fish found from Australia to Hawaii and Japan, Microcanthus strigosus, which is sometimes kept in aquaria.
Any fish in the kyphosid subfamily Microcanthinae.
Capable of being activated.
Producing balsam.
Having the health-giving properties of balsam; soothing, restorative.
Having the pleasant odour of balsam; balmy, fragrant.
ety: From balsam + -ic and French balsamique. Doublet of balsamico and piecewise doublet of balmy.

senses: someone who receives advice.
examples: Camden Citizens Advice colleagues and long-term advisees are here, some in their football gear.

senses: The third hour of daylight (about 9 am).
The service appointed for this hour.
A widow's right, where she has no conventional provision, to a liferent of a third of the husband's heritable property.
ety: Late Middle English, from Old French terce, from Latin tertia (“third; the third hour”).

senses: A heavy fall of rain.
ety: Unclear. Perhaps ultimately imitative; compare plash, pash (“heavy rain”), dialectal clash (“heavy rain”).
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:blash.

senses: The act or an act of cupellating, the assaying of a precious metal in a cupel.
A nanomolar amount or concentration
A small or female dragon.
ety: Originally a variant of dragonet. By surface analysis, dragon + -ette.

senses: Impregnation or reaction with carbon, especially in the manufacture or heat treatment of steel.
Eating many types of food.
Synonym of proactiveness.
To surrender, as a German in World War II.
ety: From German Kamerad (“comrade”), the word that a surrendering German soldier would call out.

senses: An embroidery trim made of a series of small loops.
ety: From French picot, from piquer (“to prick”).

senses: A venturi tube.
The throat of a carburetor, which is shaped so as to produce depressurization and swirling of the incoming air, allowing drops of fuel to be atomized (aerosolized).
ety: After Giovanni Battista Venturi (1746-1822), an Italian physicist who studied air flow and water flow.

senses: One who plays on a fife.
ety: From fife + -er. Piecewise doublet of piper.

senses: The quality of being sibilant: a hissing quality.
examples: The following exercises help combat sibilance, plosives, lazy tongue, and mouth problems.
A string of words beginning with ‘s’ will cause sibilance.
Work to control the sibilance of your s sounds.

senses: Divided into lanes, as with a road.
Capable of being aimed.
A man who lives in or has extensive experience of the Australian bush or outback.
examples: To A. B. Paterson, son of a dispossessed squatter, writing from a city office, the bushmen with their horses and simple skills were the backbone of Australia.
Later, historian Russel Ward (1958) famously identified the outback bushman as the “typical” Australian – a rugged individualist, courageous and loyal to his mates.

senses: The district thus inspected.
ety: From Middle English perambulacioun, from Anglo-Norman and Latin. By surface analysis, perambulate + -ation, or, by surface analysis, per- + ambulate + -ion.

senses: A triggerfish (Canthidermis sufflamen).
ety: From Middle English turbot, turbut, from Anglo-Norman turbut, Old French turbot, torbot, from Old Swedish tornbut, from törn (“thorn”) + but (“butt, flatfish”).

senses: The act or state of being a tenant.
The body of tenants on an estate.
examples: The walls were never painted during my tenantry, becoming dingier and dingier as the years went by.

senses: The part of something that has spoiled.
The process of spoiling.
examples: To prevent spoilage, store in a cool, dry place.

senses: Trainers, sneakers (sport shoes).
examples: Baby Duffy's tennies, jeans, and polo shirt--each borrowed from the grown-up vocabulary for down time--are scaled small, colored bright, and retrofitted with patches at elbow and knee.
In 1989 she performed a solo called Fame & Fortune in a pink Afro wig, a tutu, and tennies.

senses: Cooked in a tandoor.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani तन्दूरी (tandūrī) / تندوری (tandūrī), from Classical Persian تنوری (tanūrī).

senses: Having been cleared of valuable timber.
Adorable in a dorky, socially awkward manner.
A cybernetic or fully biological organism created by artificial means.
A genetically engineered humanoid-like organism created for the purpose of enslavement.
Having a single source, originating in one place at a single moment.
The topmost directory in which the files making up a web site are located on a web server.

anything which refracts light, heat or sound
The production, commerce and trade in flowers.
The art of flower arrangement.
A florist's shop.
Not medicated.
A similar venue or website for fans of a performer or band.
ety: From fan + zone: Originally a capitalized brand name for an official version of the sports venue and for the website.
examples: London Palladium in October 2022, I hosted a fanzone in The Dylan Room at the London Troubadour Club with Jackie Lees, my co-author for Bob Dylan in London.

senses: The doctrine that physical reality exists only because of the mind's awareness.
Activities such as mind-reading, especially by performers.
Oppression on the basis of neurological type or perceived intelligence.
A pitot head or pitot tube.
A forest or wood; woodland generally.
Brushwood or undergrowth, sometimes in the form of a hedge.
A hedge, especially one made from brushwood which has been wattled; also, a movable frame made from wattled branches, a hurdle.
ety: From Middle English frith (“forest, woodland; hedging”), from Old English fyrhþe, fyrhþ (“forest, wooded country; game preserve, hunting ground”), from Proto-West Germanic *furhiþi (“forest, woodland”), Proto-Germanic *furhiþją (“forest, wooded country”), *furhiþǭ, from *furhu (“fir; pine”), from *furahō, *furhō (“fir; pine; (fir or pine) forest”), from Proto-Indo-European *pérkus (“oak”), from *perkʷ- (“oak”). The English word is cognate with Latin quercus (“oak”), Old English fyrh (“fir, pine”), Old High German forst, foreht (“forest”), Old Norse fýri (“pine-wood, coniferous forest”). Latin
